cards.def: Which language is it (Old English, Middle English, or modern translation), who is speaking to whom, and where are we in the story.
Old English: the opening line of Beowulf, the narrator calling listeners to hear of the Spear-Danes' glory.

cards.term: 03. "So. The Spear-Danes in days gone by"
cards.def: Modern translation (Heaney) of Beowulf's opening, the narrator introducing the Danish kings before Shield Sheafson's funeral.

cards.term: 04. "It is always better to avenge dear ones than to indulge in mourning"
cards.def: Beowulf (Heaney): Beowulf comforts grieving Hrothgar after Grendel's mother kills Aeschere, before the fight in the mere.
Beowulf (Heaney): Hrothgar's sermon to Beowulf after the mere fight, before Beowulf sails home.

cards.term: 06. "Once the siege and assault of Troy had ceased"
cards.def: Sir Gawain (Armitage translation): the narrator's opening, tracing Britain's founding back to Troy.

cards.term: 07. "For the body which is bound within this green belt ... will be safe against anyone who seeks to strike him"
cards.def: Sir Gawain (Armitage): the lady on the third morning, offering Gawain the girdle.

cards.term: 08. "The third time, though, you strayed, / and felt my blade therefore"
cards.def: Sir Gawain (Armitage): the Green Knight at the Green Chapel explaining the nick, after the three swings.

cards.term: 09. "Here in my homelands they call me Bertilak de Hautdesert"
cards.def: Sir Gawain (Armitage): the Green Knight revealing his name and Morgan le Fay's plot to Gawain.

cards.term: 10. "Regard ... the symbol of sin, for which my neck bears the scar"
cards.def: Sir Gawain (Armitage): Gawain back at Camelot showing the girdle to the court.

cards.term: 11. "Experience, though no authority / Were in this world, is right enough for me"
cards.def: Middle English, Chaucer: the first lines of the Wife of Bath's Prologue, the Wife speaking to the pilgrims.

cards.term: 12. "A man to light a candle at his lanterne"
cards.def: Middle English, Wife of Bath's Prologue: the Wife quoting how she scolded her old husbands about their stinginess.

cards.term: 13. "Who paintede the leoun, tell me who?"
cards.def: Middle English, Wife of Bath's Prologue: the Wife attacking clerks' anti-woman books.

cards.term: 14. "Women desire to have sovereignty / As well over their husband as their love"
cards.def: Middle English, Wife of Bath's Tale: the knight's answer to the queen's court, which saves his life.

cards.term: 15. Rhymed couplets + Arthur + a knight + fairies
cards.def: Almost certainly the Wife of Bath's Tale (Chaucer), not Sir Gawain, which uses alliterative long lines and short rhyming "bob and wheel."

cards.term: 16. Alliterative lines + a short rhyming bob and wheel
cards.def: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight; the bob and wheel ends each stanza.
